content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The paper is noticing and expanding upon the connection between contrastive learning and one-class SVM. The main contribution is showing that if we see each triplet as a special form of one-class SVM, we can obtain a collection of contrastive learning approaches. This connection is later used to optimize contrastive learning using collection of one-class SVMs for very few number of triplets due to numerical complexity.

Strengths:
- The connection between one-class SVM and contrastive learning is clearly novel and interesting. It is important to understand contrastive learning and this can be impactful.

Weaknesses:
- The clarity of the paper is major problem shared by all reviewers. One would think that this might be possible to fix in camera-ready; however, authors response is not promising. First of all, authors do not update their main text for clarity during the rebuttal. More importantly, instead of noticing the clarity issue, authors claim in their message to AC/SAC that reviewers lack relevant background. The paper is about connection of two seemingly unrelated fields (one-class SVM and contrastive learning), almost no one has the full background. It is authors' responsibility to write a paper which is clear and self-contained enough so anyone can understand it. This paper is significantly far from being clear enough to general ICLR audience.

- Authors failed to demonstrate the usefulness of their method. Experiments are not convincing as they are no where near the scale of existing setups. Even more importantly, there is no path to scalability. After reading the paper, it is not clear to me how could the computational efficiency be resolved. Moreover, the theoretical insight could be useful; however, it is also not demonstrated. We do not know more about contrastive learning after this connection as no insight from one-class SVM to contrastive learning is transferred. I believe this connection is promising but it is not studied enough to be useful to neither contrastive learning nor one-class SVM.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: Interesting idea written in an unclear manner. Authors do not make any effort to improve their clarity or writing. Moreover, the idea is not executed to be useful to our community. Core of the paper is a connection between two problems but this connection does not lead into anything useful as no theoretical insight is derived. The empirical algorithm which is derived from this connection is not scalable and path to scalability is neither clear nor discussed.

content.title: Thank you for your valuable comments!
content.comment:
We will continue to improve the writing. Our responses to your questions are listed below:

1. **Smooth gradient:** We do not smooth the gradients in our approach, because each $\Delta \omega_t$ (i.e., “gradient” in our approach) is independent on the history of gradients. That is, the current gradient could be totally different from previous gradients in terms of magnitudes and orientations. The SCP procedure can be viewed as a smooth version of the loss landscape locally and approximately, but this does not mean the gradient will be smoothed. Currently our formula is based on SGD. If considering momentum, we have to change the SCP formula (i.e., the solution update part), and we do not see why our approach will not work in such cases as $\Delta \omega_t$ will still be the linear combination of $\nabla f$.

2. **Interpretation of Fig. 3:** The sparse behavior is what we expect due to the nature of SVMs. Of course, we can adjust this behavior by changing the hyperparameters in SVMs. In terms of quality, both methods assign higher weights to the triplets that can be used to reduce the loss significantly, which have a large portion of overlaps. Therefore, we believe that both methods can capture the triplet importance, but with different weighting schemes.

3. **Other alternatives:** This is a very good question, and yes, we are considering other interpretations. One possibility is using mixture models such as GMM where the assignment of each data point to the mixtures can be interpreted as linear weights in gradients. We would like to discuss with you more if you have interest.

content.title: Thank you for your valuable comments!
content.comment:
We will improve the writing. Our responses to your questions are listed below:

1. **Primal solution approximation in the one-class SVMs:** We do not analyze the primal solutions because (1) such solutions are very high-dimensional and (2) are not necessarily better than the gradients from InfoNCE or similar losses in terms of performance. Instead, we analyze the dual solutions in SVMs and show the comparison in Fig. 3. We can see that both solutions from our SVM and InfoNCE share a large portion of overlap, especially for bigger weights, which partially demonstrates our approximation hypothesis.

2. **Other constraints in Lemma 2, such as $\omega_t$:** We do not see any constraint that needs to involve $\omega_t$, as it can be viewed as an auxiliary variable and disappear in our recursive formula. Could you please clarify what constraint we need to consider besides the current ones in the lemma? Thanks.

3. **More details to support the analysis in the experiments:** Accuracy shows that our method can achieve similar performance to the competitors such as InfoNCE (if we could not, then there would be no need to make our approximation hypothesis). Triplet importance shows that the dual solutions of SVMs do produce similar weights to InfoNCE, for instance, that demonstrates our approximation hypothesis very likely to be true. Loss curves show that our SCP learning procedure can be reasonably used for network training with similar convergence pattern to InfoNCE, which demonstrates, again, our approximation hypothesis partially. Could you please clarify what more details you would like to see in our experiments? Thanks.

4. **Demo code:** We have uploaded our code online, and you can check it from https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DEEP-CONTRASTIVE-LEARNING-APPROXIMATES-ENSEMBLES-OF-ONE-CLASS-SVMS-WITH-NEURAL-TANGENT-KERNELS-BD8C/README.md

content.title: Thank you for your valuable comments!
content.comment:
We will improve the writing. Our responses to your questions are listed below:

1. **Generalization to other vision tasks, as well as other modalities beyond images:** We believe that our approach/understanding can be generalized, because all of our algorithm is about training neural networks with a contrastive learning loss. There is no dependency on either data or tasks.

2. **More details in our motivation:** In our introduction, as our motivation shown in Fig. 1, we compare two negative data augmentation methods specifically, i.e., purely random Gaussian noise (a very weak data augmentation method) and non-semantic negatives (NSN, a strong negative data augmentation method with negative selection), given the same network trained on the original data of CIFAR-10 using SimCLR with no negative data augmentation. We have done more similar experiments. For instance, we made similar observations on both CIFAR10 and STL10 using both SimCLR and MoCo v2. In forms of (dataset, method, acc), we have (CIFAR10, SimCLR+NSN, 0.64) v.s. (CIFAR10, SimCLR+Gaussian Noise, 0.65), (CIFAR10, MoCo+NSN, 0.52) v.s. (CIFAR10, MoCo+Gaussian Noise, 0.48), (STL10, SimCLR, 0.58) v.s. (STL10, SimCLR+Gaussian Noise, 0.59), (STL10, MoCo+NSN, 0.45) v.s. (STL10, MoCo+Gaussian Noise, 0.40). All are better than the baselines with no data augmentation.

3. **Our insight and experimental evaluation:** Our insight is simply that we can train a contrastive learning model using a sequence of one-class SVMs through Sequential Convex Programming (SCP), where the Lagrange multipliers serve as the linear weights for gradient calculation. Our experiments demonstrate our superior (and similar) performance with small number of triplets, similar distributions of linear weights in gradient to InfoNCE, and similar training convergence among SCP, InfoNCE and DCL. These observations well support our claim that contrastive learning can be approximately viewed as an ensemble of one-class SVMs.

content.title: Thank you for your valuable comments!
content.comment:
We will improve the writing. Our responses to your questions are listed below:

1.  **No a clear problem statement or an idea of the proposed approach in the introduction:** On Page 2 in the bold font, “So how shall we measure "triplet importance"?” shows exactly our problem, and on the same page “In contrast, we interpret contrastive learning as a Sequential Convex Programming (SCP) problem where each sub-problem is a one-class SVM” shows exactly our approach.

2. **Generality of Fig. 1:** We made similar observations on both CIFAR10 and STL10 using both SimCLR and MoCo v2. In forms of (dataset, method, acc), we have (CIFAR10, SimCLR+NSN, 0.64) v.s. (CIFAR10, SimCLR+Gaussian Noise, 0.65), (CIFAR10, MoCo+NSN, 0.52) v.s. (CIFAR10, MoCo+Gaussian Noise, 0.48), (STL10, SimCLR, 0.58) v.s. (STL10, SimCLR+Gaussian Noise, 0.59), (STL10, MoCo+NSN, 0.45) v.s. (STL10, MoCo+Gaussian Noise, 0.40). All are better than the baselines with no data augmentation. These results shows the generality of our motivative figure, while in the introduction we just illustrates one case.

3. **Related Work:** We will improve this part, but in current version each subsection in related work is associated with a key word in our approach, and thus they are highly relevant.

4.  **Readability of Sec. 3.1:** We will improve it. In this section, we shows the background for understanding our approach later, and draw comparison between the contrastive learning and one-class svm, as shown on the top of Page 5.

5. **Lemmas and proofs in Sec. 3.3:** Lemma 1 shows that $\omega^*$ will be bounded, and based on this, Lemma 2 shows the connections between contrastive learning and one-class svm, which is one of our key contributions. 

6. **It stays unclear if the huge additional effort finally pays off?** This is a very good question and we wish that we could answer it. However, as we clearly stated in the paper, on Page 8 “Though the computational burden of the per-sample gradient in Eq. 7 prevents us from doing more experiments on a larger number of samples, the point is made clear that many one-class SVM updates could approximate the deep contrastive learning based on the behavior of our experiments.” The total number of triplets is 16,256 which is far beyond the number that our hardware can afford. We are working on this problem now.

7. **Bibliography:** We will improve it.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper on hand tackles the problem of deep contrastive learning, by showing that existing loss functions are related to one-class SVMs. Even though this interesting aspect is not fully clear, this seems to be a reasonable contribution, which is illustrated in a small experimental setup.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

The overall idea seems to valuable, in particular since the problem is addressed from a theoretical points of view.


Weaknesses:

The overall presentation is weak and the paper is hard to read. In addition, the experimental results are interesting but leave open many questions.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The presented approach seems to be novel, however, due to the structure and the quality of the presentation neither the technical details (for a re-implementation)  nor the benefits from an experimental point of view are clear. The most relevant points are given below:

Due to the structure of the of the introduction neither a clear problem statement nor an idea of the proposed approach is apparent.

The conclusions drawn from the experiment shown in Fig.1 would not hold in general. This is just a single example from which no general propertied can be deduced.

The related works section does not really discuss related work. Here mainly general references given, which are not directly related to the work on hand.

Sec.3.1 is not structured very well. In this way, there is no reading and argumentation flow. Moreover, due to large number of mathematical terms it might be better to use more separated equations to improve the readability.

Sec.3.3 is a sequence of lemmas and proofs but it takes some effort to understand how these are related to rest of the presentation.

In general, Sec.3 would need to be restructured to increase the readability.

Even though the results indicate an improvement to the baselines, the benefits are not fully clear. In particular, it stays unclear if the huge additional effort finally pays off? A more thorough evaluation would be required.

The bibliography needs to be seriously checked for consistency and correctness.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a novel analysis that explains and models the importance of negative samples for contrastive learning. Specifically, they bring back the one-class Support Vector Machines (SVMs) and showed that the gradient of typical contrastive loss functions ensembles the solution of a mixture of per-triplet one-class SVM problems. The authors then proposed a novel algorithm to compute the contrastive gradients and showed its effectiveness on a set of benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The analysis on connecting SVMs and contrastive learning is novel and can potentially help understand why contrastive learning works.

Weakness:
- The proposed algorithm solves a one-class SVM problem w.r.t. a set of per-triplet gradients $\nabla f_i(w_t)$. The resulting output gradient behaves like a smoothed version of all per-triplet gradients. I wonder how it compares with the momentum methods and/or some gradient smoothing / variance reduction techniques. This should help the readers to understand the proposed algorithm.
- How should we interpret figure 3? It seems that the proposed importance is much sparser compared to the InfoNCE importance. Is it expected? What else can we tell about the quality of the importance based on this figure?
- It seems that right part of eq (3) essentially is just a linear combination. From that, it is not obvious why one-class SVMs should be chosen to model the contrastive gradient. Have the authors considered other alternatives?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
As far as I can tell, the presentation and organization of the paper is pretty good. One thing to improve is that sub-section 3.3 is a little disconnected with the context. The whole sub-section is proving theorems without stating clearly why they are needed.

The analysis and the experimental results look sound to me.

I think the idea of connecting contrastive loss to one-class SVMs is novel but the choice also needs to be explained (why other alternatives are not chosen).

The paper proposed an algorithm and I'm confident to reproduce it.
content.summary_of_the_review: In general, I think the quality of this paper is good except several explanations need to be made.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Proposing a novel  sequential convex programming (SCP) algorithm for contrastive learning, and each sub-problem is a one-class SVM. 
2. Combining the one-class SVM with the neural tangent kernel.

Weaknesses:
1. The expression is difficult to understant.
2.  I mainly  concern obout  the details of the theoretical proof, such as the constraints on initialization in the NTK, and the details of Lemma 2.
3. The experiments do not fully support the theoretical analysis in the section 3.3.

content.summary_of_the_review:
1. Please impove the expression of this paper. For example 'in the paper we show that a model learned by deep contrastive learning with a family of loss functions such as InfoNCE essentially approximates an ensemble of one-class support vector machines (SVMs) with neural tangent kernels (NTKs)' in the abstract and ' where our loss curve is linearly scaled by 5 for a better view' in the last paragraph of section 4.3.
2. In the Figure 4, authors report the the loss curves boased on three different methods, and analyze that all the methods are convergent, which also supports their analysis of primal solution approximation in the one-class SVMs. Figure 4 only show that the loss of all the methos are convergent, and it is not obvious show the analysis on the primal solution approximation in the one-class SVMs. 
3. In Lemma 2, authors show a approximation theory.  Are there any other constraints on the validity of the conclusion, such as the $w_t$. 
4. For the experiment, authors report the accuracy, triplet importance, and the loss curves. These results can not support the analysis in section 3.2 and 3.3. Please giving more details to support the analysis.

content.title: Deep Contrastive Learning Approximates Ensembles of One-Class SVMs with Neural Tangent Kernels
content.abstract: To demystify the (self-supervised) contrastive learning in representation learning, in the paper we show that a model learned by deep contrastive learning with a family of loss functions such as InfoNCE essentially approximates an ensemble of one-class support vector machines (SVMs) with neural tangent kernels (NTKs). This result comes from the fact that each gradient for network weight update in contrastive learning can be interpreted approximately as the primal solution for a one-class SVM with contrastive gradients as input. From the dual perspective, the Lagrange multipliers provide unique insights into the importance of the anchor-positive-negative triplet samples. In this way, we further propose a novel sequential convex programming (SCP) algorithm for contrastive learning, where each sub-problem is a one-class SVM. Empirically we demonstrate that our approach can learn better gradients than conventional contrastive learning approaches that significantly improve performance.
